attribution.note: Zitron's own framing as author. He quotes Zuckerberg's words, but the pivot assertion is his.

semantics.note: Adding 'from the metaverse' is implied by the context (the name change, 'again'). The less-than-two-years timing and the AI-as-largest-investment framing are kept.

contract.note: Reading 'pivoting' as a shift in publicly emphasised priority, not abandonment, is an ordinary and fair plain reading. Testing the company's own characterisation matches what the speaker cited.

evidence.note: Rebrand on 2021-10-28 with a metaverse focus. Sets the baseline and the timing.
On 2023-03-14 Zuckerberg called AI the single largest investment. That is under 18 months after the rebrand and before the post.
Shows metaverse work continued in Dec 2022. This fits a shift in emphasis rather than abandonment.

reviews.rationale: The rebrand was in Oct 2021. By March 2023 Zuckerberg publicly named AI Meta's single largest investment, a clear change in emphasis from the metaverse focus announced at the rebrand, and within two years. Continued metaverse work does not undercut a pivot read as a change in emphasis.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: The cancellation and cost motive are firm. The transfer of savings to AI is an explicit assumption ('I assume'), so it is hedged and not scored.

contract.note: 'Big plans for AR glasses' is ambiguous: it could mean the Nazare consumer release or the whole program. Separating the two components is fair.

evidence.note: June 2022: the planned 2024 Nazare consumer release was dropped amid reported cost cutting ('could not afford' some projects).
Feb 2023 roadmap: thousands of staff still building AR glasses, with devices planned through 2027. The broader program was not cancelled.

reviews.rationale: Holds: Meta cancelled the consumer release of its first AR glasses (Nazare) amid cost cutting. Fails: the broader AR-glasses plans continued, with a roadmap through 2027. The assumed redirection of savings to AI is hedged and not adjudicable.

semantics.note: The core is that Zuckerberg abandoned the metaverse once AI became the trend. 'The second' is rhetorical immediacy.

contract.note: 'Give up on the idea' ordinarily means abandonment. Testing for continued substantive pursuit in March 2023 is a fair plain reading.

evidence.note: Bloomberg: on 2023-03-29 Meta held a press briefing inside Horizon Workrooms and said it was in the metaverse 'for the long haul'. This shows continued pursuit.

reviews.rationale: In late March 2023 Meta was still running and showcasing its metaverse products and publicly restating a long-term commitment, as independently reported by Bloomberg. That contradicts the claim that Zuckerberg had given up on the metaverse by the time of the post.

semantics.note: 'May seem strange' is a rhetorical concession, not a hedge on the claim. The claim presupposes that the metaverse was dropped and asserts a track record of failed imitations.

contract.note: Splitting the claim into metaverse abandonment and a record of repeated failed copies is fair. Reading 'track record' as repeated instances, not universal failure, is an ordinary reading.

evidence.note: Poke was Facebook's Snapchat clone. It failed to gain users and was pulled in 2014.
Slingshot was modelled on Snapchat. It failed to catch on and was withdrawn in 2015.
On 2023-04-18 Meta expanded Horizon Worlds to teens. The metaverse was not dropped by the time of the post.
Heavy Reels use limits any sweeping claim that Meta cannot compete. It does not erase the earlier failures.

reviews.rationale: The track-record part holds: Poke and Slingshot were Snapchat copies that failed and were withdrawn. The premise that he dropped the metaverse fails: Meta was expanding Horizon Worlds two days before the post. The Wall Street motive is not established.
